items.title: PMD predicts more rain in upper regions over the weekend, including Islamabad
items.description: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) issued a weather advisory on Wednesday predicting more rain in the upper regions of the country over the weekend, particularly in the Potohar region and Islamabad. The Met office said that monsoon currents were penetrating the upper parts of the country, according to the advisory issued at 3pm on Wednesday. It added that a westerly wave was also affecting these regions and likely to strengthen on September 4-5 (Friday and Saturday). Under the influence of this weather system, it said that rain-wind and thundershowers — with isolated heavy falls — were expected in Kashmir’s Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur from Thursday to Sunday, with occasional gaps. In Gilgit-Baltistan, the same is expected in Diamer, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar during the same time period. Rain-wind and thundershowers “with scattered heavy falls, at times very heavy” were forecast in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Peshawar, Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Malakand, Mardan, Nowshera, Charsadda, Swabi, Shangla, Battagram, Buner, Kohat, Hangu, Kurram, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Orakzai, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Karak, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Dera Ismail Khan, Bannu and Waziristan, from the evening of Sep 3 to Sep 5 with occasional gaps. In Islamabad and upper Punjab, similar thundershowers and isolated heavy or very heavy falls were predicted in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galliyat, Jhelum, Chakwal, Talagang, Attock, Lahore, Sialkot, Sheikhupura, Narowal, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Wazirabad, Hafizabad and Kasur from Sep 3-5. The PMD forecast the same in Okara, Nankana Sahib, Sargodha, Khushab, Mianwali, Noorpur Thal, Faisalabad, Jhang, Toba Tek Singh, Layyah, Bhakkar, Sahiwal, Dera Ghazi Khan and the surrounding areas between Sep 4-5 with occasional gaps. The Met Office added that “mainly hot and humid weather” would prevail in most parts of Sindh and Balochistan during the forecast period, but noted that rain-wind and thunderstorms were expected in Zhob, Bar Khan, Musakhel and the surrounding areas. The PMD advisory warned that the heavy rains may cause urban flooding in low-lying areas of Islamabad and Rawalpindi, as well as Peshawar, Mardan, Swabi, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Sialkot, Faisalabad and Lahore on Friday and Saturday. It also warned of flash flooding in local streams and nullahs in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Shangla, Battagram, Buner, Malakand, Mansehra, Abbottabad, GB, Kashmir, Murree, Galliyat and the twin cities during the forecast period. “Landslides may occur in hilly areas of KP, GB, Murree, Galliyat and Kashmir during the forecast period,” it added, advising tourists and travellers to “remain cautious”. The PMD also advised farmers to manage their crop activities in view of the weather conditions. It asked all concerned authorities to remain alert and take necessary measures to avoid untoward situations. Heavy rain has already been lashing Rawalpindi and Islamabad this week, inundating low-lying areas on Tuesday morning and raising the water level in Leh Nullah. On Monday, about two hours of heavy showers caused rainwater to accumulate in streets and low-lying areas of Rawalpindi, turning roads into small ponds. Many cars and motorcycles were seen stranded in rainwater.

items.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum tests democratic future
items.description: Following voter approval of a constitutional change that expands presidential powers, Guinea-Bissau faces renewed debate over legitimacy, civilian rule and democratic safeguards.

items.title: China's Xi urges new Middle East security framework during Egypt visit
items.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping called on Middle Eastern nations to oppose external interference and consider reshaping the region’s security order during a visit to Egypt on Wednesday, as Beijing seeks to expand its influence amid the US-Israeli war against Iran. Xi’s first trip to the Middle East in four years comes as US partners in the region reassess their strategic relationships after months of conflict that have disrupted trade, shaken economies and raised questions about Washington’s long-term role. Egypt, itself a major US defence partner that receives around $1.3 billion annually in military aid from Washington, has been steadily increasing economic and military cooperation with China in recent years. Members of the Egyptian honour guard before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at Cairo International Airport for an official visit to Egypt in Cairo, Egypt on September 1, 2026. —Reuters/File Welcomed by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi with a military ceremony in Cairo, Xi said countries in the region should be “masters of their own destiny” and explore a new regional “security architecture”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua . Xi also said China was ready to work with regional countries to safeguard shipping routes, an issue that has taken on greater importance after conflict disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb . The leaders agreed to deepen security cooperation and counterterrorism coordination, Xinhua said. The two sides also agreed to expand cooperation in data centers, semiconductors and critical metals supply chains and strengthen the use of each other’s currencies in trade and investment, according to a joint statement. ‘Strategic balance’ For Egypt, stronger ties with China fit a broader effort to diversify international partnerships. In an article published ahead of the visit, Sisi said Egypt pursued a policy of “strategic balance” at a time of growing global rivalry. “Egypt wants to widen the circle of its relations with major world powers, including China,” former Egyptian diplomat Ayman Zaineldine told Reuters . “So the visions converge.” China’s President Xi Jinping walks with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi followed by their wives Peng Liyuan and Entissar Amer upon their arrival at the Cairo International Airport, Egypt on September 1, 2026. —Reuters/File For China, Egypt’s regional influence and strategic location make it an important partner as Beijing seeks a broader economic role and tries to chip away at US influence in the region. “Egypt represents something quite valuable to Beijing — a large domestic market for investment opportunities, and a lot of diplomatic weight in the region, including the Palestine question, as well as connectivity to Africa,” said H.A. Hellyer, a scholar at the Royal United Services Institute think tank. Growing military ties were on display last month during Egypt’s “Eagles of Civilisation” exercises with China, which included a rare air combat drill involving Chinese-made J-16 jets and French-made Rafale aircraft. China’s President Xi Jinping (center L) along with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and their wives Peng Liyuan and Entissar Amer watch Egyptian artists performing during a welcome ceremony at the Cairo International Airport on September 1, 2026. —AFP/File Enthusiasm for the Chinese president’s visit has been evident for days in Egypt’s capital, where streets have been decked out in Chinese flags and images of iconic sites including Egypt’s Sphinx and China’s Great Wall. Economic ties expand Home to the Suez Canal and a population of more than 110 million, Egypt is an important market for China, importing some $10 billion of Chinese goods in the first half of this year alone. Chinese investment has risen rapidly since Sisi visited China and signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2014, with Chinese companies pouring billions into container ports, green hydrogen projects and facilities to make iron pipes, car tyres and satellites. Cars drive in traffic beneath a large screen displaying portraits of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and China’s President Xi Jinping, along with a message reading in Arabic, “The Egyptian-Chinese friendship welcomes Egypt’s guest, His Excellency President Xi Jinping, President of the People’s Republic of China,” in Cairo, Egypt, on September 1, 2026. —Reuters/File Egypt’s cabinet says the Suez Canal Economic Zone has attracted about $4 billion in Chinese investment. On Wednesday, Egyptian authorities announced plans to expand a Chinese-developed industrial area in the zone, while ZC Rubber Group signed a preliminary agreement to study a $500 million tyre making complex.

items.title: Sacrés face au Nigeria, les Étalons U20 ouvrent-ils une nouvelle ère pour le football burkinabè ?
items.description: Un vent de fraîcheur souffle sur le football burkinabè avec la victoire retentissante des Étalons U20 au tournoi UFOA-B 2026. Face à l’une des équipes les plus redoutables de la sous-région, le Nigeria, ces jeunes talents ont imposé leur statut en s’imposant sur un score sans appel de 4-1. Ce succès, qui fait écho à la victoire précédente en phase de groupes, traduit bien plus qu’un simple triomphe sportif : il pourrait bien marquer le début d’une nouvelle dynamique à long terme pour une jeunesse burkinabè animée d’un esprit de conquête inédit. Au-delà de la victoire, c’est une véritable rupture qui s’esquisse. En effet, ces jeunes joueurs menés par Oscar Barro semblent incarner une génération d’espoir capable de poser les bases solides d’un football burkinabè en pleine renaissance. La qualification directe à la prochaine CAN U20 au Ghana leur offre une scène élargie pour confirmer leur montée en puissance et faire rayonner leur équipe nationale sur le continent. Le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré , a également félicité les joueurs et le staff, saluant une performance qui fait la fierté de la Nation. Une aubaine pour les opérateurs de jeux qui proposent des avantages aux joueurs. À ce titre, le code promo Betwinner au Burkina peut être consulté comme information pratique en parallèle de l’actualité footballistique. Il suffit de l’utiliser intelligemment pour rehausser ces bonus et aborder les jeux sur le match du Burkina et autres en toute sécurité. Nos experts ont d’ailleurs pu le tester et confirmer sa validité. Un triomphe sans précédent face au Nigeria : les Étalons U20 imposent leur domination Le 9 août 2026 à Yamoussoukro, la confrontation entre les Étalons U20 du Burkina Faso et les Flying Eagles du Nigeria n’a pas tenu ses promesses en termes de suspense. Dès l’entame du match, les Burkinabè ont affiché une détermination absolue, marquant trois buts décisifs en un quart d’heure seulement. Alassane Bagayogo s’est illustré dès la troisième minute en ouvrant le score, signe d’une équipe agressive et bien préparée. Le rapide doublé d’Achraf Lookman Tapsoba à la quatrième minute a ancré cette assurance offensive, avant qu’Issoufou Dabo ne confirme la supériorité burkinabè sur un corner à la 14ème minute. Le Burkina Faso a surtout fait la différence par son entame très intense, ses transitions rapides et son efficacité offensive, avec trois buts inscrits avant la pause. Ce succès écrasant révèle aussi une maîtrise collective impressionnante, qui a laissé peu d’espace aux Nigérians pour s’exprimer. Le manque de réaction immédiate des Flying Eagles face à l’avalanche de buts témoigne d’un Burkina Faso serein et concentré. Si le Nigeria a réussi à réduire l’écart par un penalty en seconde période, la réponse immédiate d’un sublime coup franc de plus de 30 mètres signé Fadel Barro a clos tout espoir de retour pour les Nigérians. Le score final de 4-1 reflète non seulement la supériorité burkinabè lors de ce match, mais aussi une volonté affichée de conquérir un titre longtemps resté hors de portée pour cette génération. Ce triomphe ne s’est pas fait au hasard. Il est le fruit d’un travail rigoureux tant sur le plan tactique que mental. Oscar Barro, en sélectionneur averti, a su galvaniser ses troupes en exploitant pleinement les qualités individuelles et collectives de ses joueurs. Les Étalons U20 ont ainsi su allier vitesse, technique et rigueur défensive pour dominer leur adversaire. Cette victoire, première dans l’histoire du Burkina Faso au tournoi UFOA-B, crée une dynamique positive qui pourra se traduire dans les compétitions à venir, notamment la CAN U20 2027. Une jeunesse dorée : comment les Étalons U20 incarnent le renouveau du football burkinabè Ce succès retentissant met en lumière un phénomène plus large : la montée en puissance d’une jeunesse burkinabè ambitieuse et talentueuse sur laquelle le football national peut désormais s’appuyer. Dans un contexte où le football burkinabè a longtemps souffert d’un déficit de résultats internationaux, cette génération de joueurs semble porter un souffle nouveau, marquant un véritable tournant. Le travail de formation mené dans les centres de jeunes talents commence à porter ses fruits avec des joueurs comme Alassane Bagayogo, élu homme du match, dont les qualités offensives et le sens du but incarnent l’avenir de cette sélection. À ses côtés, Louckman Tapsoba et Issouf Dabo affichent une complémentarité et une maturité tactique qui tranchent avec les générations précédentes. De plus, la présence de figures talentueuses comme Fadel Barro, auteur d’un coup franc spectaculaire, témoigne du potentiel technique que la formation burkinabè s’efforce de développer. Ce renouveau ne se limite pas au terrain. Il se manifeste aussi par un esprit collectif renforcé et une stratégie globale élaborée par Oscar Barro, dont l’approche bâtie autour d’une discipline rigoureuse et d’une cohésion soudée semble porter ses fruits. Les Étalons U20 montrent ainsi que c’est possible d’allier individualités prometteuses et travail d’équipe pour produire un football séduisant et efficace. Le gagnant de cette dynamique est bien sûr le football burkinabè dans sa globalité, qui peut aspirer à une reconnaissance renouvelée sur la scène africaine et internationale. Par ailleurs, cette jeunesse dorée offre au pays un espoir concret pour l’avenir, avec des retombées positives également en termes économiques et sociaux, renforçant l’attrait du football comme vecteur d’unité et d’émancipation des jeunes. Principaux facteurs du succès des Étalons U20 Une formation axée sur la technique et la tactique : axée dès le plus jeune âge sur les fondamentaux du jeu. Un encadrement complice : Oscar Barro et son staff instaurent un climat de confiance et d’exigence. Une cohésion renforcée : esprit collectif irréprochable, gage de solides résultats sur le terrain. La qualité des infrastructures : modernisation des centres de formation jeunesse. Le soutien fédéral et politique : mobilisation des autorités autour du projet sportif. Le rôle de la victoire à l’UFOA-B dans la consolidation du football burkinabè Remporter le tournoi UFOA-B ne se limite pas à empocher un trophée ; c’est un véritable tremplin qui permet aux Étalons U20 et au football burkinabè d’asseoir une nouvelle crédibilité. Cette compétition régionale, très disputée, est un baromètre essentiel pour jauger le niveau des jeunes talents ouest-africains et leurs capacités à s’imposer sur la scène continentale. Pour le Burkina Faso, inscrire son nom au palmarès en 2026 est une marque claire de progression et de maturité. Les Étalons U20 avaient déjà attisé les attentes, mais c’est cette victoire éclatante face au Nigeria, un adversaire traditionnellement dominant, qui vient véritablement confirmer cette montée en puissance. Elle participe à bâtir une confiance collective et un état d’esprit conquérant chez les jeunes joueurs, indispensables pour les échéances à venir, notamment la CAN U20 2027. Outre les aspects sportifs, cette victoire a également des répercussions sur le plan institutionnel et économique. Le succès des Étalons U20 pourrait attirer l’attention des sponsors, médias et investisseurs, cherchant à associer leur image à une équipe évoluant dans une direction ascendante. Pour la Fédération Burkinabè de Football, c’est aussi une offre d’opportunité unique qui peut renforcer ses politiques de développement, de formation et de gestion des talents, avec des retombées positives à moyen terme. Enfin, la visibilité acquise par cette victoire alimente la ferveur du public et redonne espoir aux supporters et acteurs du football national. L’engouement suscité par ce sacre pourrait stimuler la pratique du football dans les écoles et les quartiers, assurant ainsi un vivier de talents encore plus large pour les années à venir. Étalons U20 et CAN 2027 : perspectives et enjeux pour la jeunesse burkinabè Qualifiés pour la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations U20 au Ghana en 2027, les Étalons U20 savent que ce nouveau défi sera une occasion cruciale pour asseoir leur stature continentale. Ce passage obligé révèle le niveau de compétition supérieur et de pression qu’ils devront affronter. Le Burkina Faso, grâce à cette génération, nourrit de grandes ambitions, tant dans la quête du titre que dans la consolidation de son projet sportif. Cette participation directe à la CAN U20 ouvre des perspectives multiples pour la jeunesse burkinabè. Sur le plan sportif, c’est un tremplin important qui, en cas de succès, pourrait permettre à plusieurs jeunes joueurs d’attirer l’attention des recruteurs internationaux, ouvrant ainsi la voie à des carrières professionnelles en Europe ou ailleurs. Sur le plan institutionnel, la fédération devra s’appuyer sur cette génération pour structurer des actions de développement à plus long terme, en optimisant la détection des talents, le suivi médical et la préparation mentale des joueurs. La CAN U20 pourra également servir de laboratoire tactique pour l’ équipe nationale senior , en intégrant progressivement ces jeunes pépites au sein du groupe professionnel. Le défi sera donc double : maintenir la dynamique positive et gérer la pression liée aux attentes. Les joueurs et le staff devront utiliser cette compétition pour acquérir de l’expérience, affiner leur jeu et concrétiser un projet fédérateur porté par une ambition commune pour le football burkinabè. Tableau des objectifs clés pour la CAN U20 2027 Objectif Description Impact attendu Performance sportive Atteindre au moins les demi-finales. Renforcer la crédibilité internationale de la sélection U20. Détection et valorisation Identifier des talents susceptibles d’intégrer la sélection senior. Assurer la relève de l’équipe nationale A. Image et sponsorisation Augmenter la visibilité et attirer les partenariats économiques. Renforcer l’infrastructure financière autour du football burkinabè. Formation mentale Préparer les joueurs à gérer la pression des grandes compétitions. Optimiser la résilience et le professionnalisme des jeunes. Analyse tactique : quelles leçons tirer de la victoire des Étalons U20 face au Nigeria ? La démonstration des Étalons U20 en finale du tournoi UFOA-B donne lieu à une riche analyse tactique, révélatrice des forces et axes d’amélioration du football burkinabè. Dès le coup d’envoi, l’équipe a choisi un système offensif ambitieux, adopté par Oscar Barro , reposant sur une pression haute et une exploitation rapide des espaces derrière la défense adverse. Le double but en tout début de match traduit la réussite de ce plan, avec des relances rapides vers Alassane Bagayogo et Achraf Lookman Tapsoba, dont la vitesse a fait vaciller la ligne nigériane. La variété des attaques passant aussi bien par le centre que par les ailes – démontre une maîtrise tactique remarquable pour un groupe U20 et témoigne d’une préparation approfondie. La capacité à profiter d’un coup de pied arrêté (le but de Dabo sur corner) montre aussi une bonne organisation défensive et offensive. Ce système a permis de mettre le Nigeria en difficulté, l’adversaire n’ayant jamais pu établir son propre rythme, faute notamment d’un milieu de terrain capable de rivaliser physiquement et techniquement. Toutefois, la réduction sur penalty en 2e mi-temps souligne une légère vulnérabilité défensive sur les phases arrêtées, point à travailler d’urgence avant la CAN U20. Le but de la dernière minute inscrit sur coup franc illustre quant à lui une indiscipline nigériane face à un anxiété psychologique palpable dans le final du match. Il convient aussi de saluer la prestation du gardien Rahim Ouattara, élu meilleur gardien du tournoi, qui a parfaitement géré les phases de match plus tendues. Sa sérénité dans les sorties et sa lecture du jeu ont apporté un dernier rempart rassurant qui a conforté la confiance collective. Cette prestation homogène participe de la solidité d’ensemble visible dans cette équipe. Points forts et axes d’amélioration clé Points forts : pression haute, rapidité offensive, coups de pied arrêtés bien maîtrisés, gardien décisif. Axes d’amélioration : gestion des phases arrêtées défensives, renforcements du milieu de terrain, conservation du ballon sous pression. Organisation collective : cohésion tactique et discipline dans le placement. FAQ Quels joueurs ont brillé lors de la finale UFOA-B 2026 ? Alassane Bagayogo a été élu homme du match, Mohamed Zongo le meilleur joueur du tournoi, et Rahim Ouattara le meilleur gardien. Ces joueurs ont marqué les esprits par leur performance exceptionnelle lors de la finale et tout au long de la compétition. Quelles sont les retombées économiques de cette victoire pour le football burkinabè ? La victoire crée un attrait accru pour les sponsors et investisseurs, permettant une meilleure infrastructure et des ressources pour la formation et la compétition des jeunes talents du Burkina Faso. Que représente cette victoire pour l’équipe nationale burkinabè à long terme ? Ce sacre marque une étape importante dans la consolidation d’une équipe nationale jeune et compétitive, promettant une relève solide pour les sélections seniors dans les années à venir. Quels défis attendent les Étalons U20 à la CAN 2027 ? Les Étalons U20 devront confirmer leur progression en affrontant des équipes de haut niveau, tout en gérant la pression liée aux attentes pour atteindre un niveau de performance élevé. L’article Sacrés face au Nigeria, les Étalons U20 ouvrent-ils une nouvelle ère pour le football burkinabè ? est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Experts call for multisectoral approach, community-led intervention in addressing malnutrition crisis
items.description: Day 1 of the two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’ — held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel — concluded on Wednesday, with experts urging urgent action on Pakistan’s malnutrition and stunting crisis, with a focus on multisectoral interventions. With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations. View the full agenda here . 5:27pm - Day 1 of the conference concludes 5:15pm - Researcher calls for nutrition-related interventions at community, systemic levels Director at the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood said focus on nutrition was needed at the community, systemic, and legislative levels. Remarking on awareness campaigns on the community level, she said, “Interventions are not designed according to the latest theories and latest approaches towards designing behaviour change”. She stressed a multisectoral approach to nutrition, adding that “no specific industry owns nutrition”. 5:00pm - Doctor stresses rigorous testing for pregnant women Dr Nosheen Ashraf of the National Institutes of Health, speaking about maternal nutrition, said that during antenatal visits, mothers are asked to take supplements to address nutritional deficiencies; however, she noted a lack of consistent monitoring. Dr Ashraf said there were not enough laboratories in far-flung areas, as she called for rigorous testing of pregnant mothers to track any nutritional deficiencies. 4:55pm - Gynaecologist stresses nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth Capital Hospital Associate Gynaecologist Dr Urooj Yasir Khan said the focus of nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth. “There is hardly any awareness about nutrition in our adolescent girl groups.” Following a substantial loss of iron during menstruation, micronutrient deficiencies in the body at the onset of pregnancy, especially if it’s a teenage pregnancy, can lead to growth-restricted babies, she said. Commenting on treatment for obesity, she said, “we don’t say what’s important to eat”, adding that the focus seems to be on the number of calories consumed. 4:53pm - Founder Nutradevice calls for equitable access to nutritious food Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi held that creating awareness about nutritious food did not guarantee nutrition; rather, she maintained that it was worth examining “if the mother can access it, implement it, afford it and keeping in view the power of the woman in the household, can she give it to the children”. Dr Taqvi also clarified misconceptions around nutrition. “It is not true that healthy food is always expensive [..] as you don’t always have to focus on animal-based food”. She also noted that mothers in Pakistani households did not prioritise themselves. “Food is given to the family first. and then the mother eats whatever is left of it.” She also noted that stigma around weight gain was leading to nutritional deficiencies in women as well. Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi speaks at the conference. — White Star 4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition. “The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said. She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage. “During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition. “250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said. Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood at the conference. — White Star 4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins Panelists at the session titled ‘The first 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’. — White Star 4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”. “Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said. Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem. 3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”. He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential. He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps… that will allow […] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.” Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Muhammad Asim 3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce. He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition. He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc. 3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition. “We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled. “It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added. “Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added. Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Muhammad Asim 3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun. 3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue. “Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting. “ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.” Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’ The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”. Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition. “Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said. 3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”. “We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said. Panelists at the Building Human Capital and Driving Economic Growth. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits. Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later. He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic. “If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said. 2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’ Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”. “The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said. 2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’ Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue. “Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.” “There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added. Panelists at the session titled ‘Building Human Capital and Driving Economic Growth’ at the conference. — White Star 2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’ The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”. “Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition. “It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added. 2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break 1:50pm - Lunch break The conference will resume at 2:30pm. 1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’ Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition. “As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”. She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition. Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty. “It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said. 1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition. She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”. “Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said. She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”. “If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said. Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important. She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions. 1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food. “It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said. He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said. Thomas Conan. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry. He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”. “This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021. “Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer. “So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said. 12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity. “We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy. “Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues. At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.” Benazir Income Support Programme Chairperson Senator Rubina Khalid delivers the keynote address. — DawnNewsTV 12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins. 12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world. “We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”. “In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India. “So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.” 12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges. “If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition. He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity. “So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention. “We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said. Dr Irshad Danish. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme. “It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership. “These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.” 11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region. “We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said. He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things. Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzed 11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun. 11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform. “It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”. “We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted. Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”. He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition. “The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said. 11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’ Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow. “Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said. 11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement. She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”. Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition. “This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added. Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries. “Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said. The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.” She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”. 11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone. “Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said. “Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said. 11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition. “Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said. He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience. “Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems. 10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins The session on global and regional realities has now begun. 10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting. “Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said. She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes. “Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said. ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’ Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”. “When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said. She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases. 10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations. “When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required. 10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food. “It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said. World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity. “Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action. 10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today. “It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said. “We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action. “Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said. 10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity “Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. “Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues. “90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said. “If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said. “That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said. 9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority. He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development. “We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said. “Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said. 9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either. “You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said. “With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said. “That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added. Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”. “We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said. “So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added. She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”. 9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’ In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted. “These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said. “And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said. 9:45am - Conference begins The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran. Attendees of the Act For Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Agriculture: une jeune brevetée met son expertise au service du champ familial
items.description: BURKINA-SANDBONDTENGA- AGRICULTURE-EXPERTISE Sandbondtenga/Agriculture: une jeune brevetée met son expertise au service du champ familial Korsimoro, 2 sept. 2026 (AIB)- Zonabo Sawadogo, jeune titulaire d’un Brevet d’études professionnelles (BEP) en agronomie, met ses compétences au service de l’exploitation familiale à Korsimoro, dans la province du Sandbondtenga, contribuant à améliorer les pratiques culturales et la qualité de la production. Élève au Lycée professionnel régional Nazi Boni de Dédougou, la jeune agronome consacre ses vacances scolaires aux travaux champêtres. Elle y met en pratique les connaissances théoriques et techniques acquises au cours de sa formation, notamment dans la conduite des cultures. « Nous l’apprécions beaucoup. Elle est travailleuse et elle nous aide avec les bonnes techniques agricoles », a témoigné son père, Sita Sawadogo, qui attribue en partie la bonne physionomie de son champ à l’apport technique de sa fille et espère une bonne récolte. Pour Zonabo Sawadogo, le champ familial constitue également un espace d’apprentissage et d’expérimentation où elle peut confronter ses connaissances aux réalités du terrain. Son engagement suscite l’admiration du voisinage. « Voir une fille se donner tant aux travaux champêtres et avec succès est encourageant. Zonabo est à féliciter », a confié Mamou Ouédraogo, une voisine. Passionnée d’agriculture, la jeune fille dit avoir été davantage motivée par l’appel des autorités à renforcer la production nationale et à œuvrer pour l’autosuffisance alimentaire. « L’agriculture est une passion pour moi et l’appel du président du Faso à travailler pour l’atteinte de l’autosuffisance alimentaire a encore ravivé cette passion », a-t-elle expliqué. Après son BEP, Zonabo Sawadogo ambitionne de poursuivre sa formation et de décrocher le Baccalauréat professionnel Agriculture en 2027, avec l’objectif de renforcer davantage ses compétences et de contribuer au développement d’une agriculture productive et durable. Agence d’Information du Burkina OZ/aio/bak

items.title: Houet : la commune de Bobo-Dioulasso réaffirme son attachement aux symboles nationaux
items.description: Houet : la commune de Bobo-Dioulasso réaffirme son attachement aux symboles nationaux Bobo-Dioulasso, 2 sept. 2026 (AIB) – La commune de Bobo-Dioulasso a réaffirmé, ce mercredi, son attachement aux symboles de la Nation, à l’occasion de la cérémonie communale mensuelle de montée des couleurs nationales, tenue à la mairie de l’arrondissement n°3. La cérémonie a été présidé par le premier Vice-président de la délégation spéciale de la commune (PDS), Moussa Sanou représentant le PDS. Il a indiqué que cette cérémonie mensuelle constitue « un moment de rassemblement, de communion et de renouvellement de notre engagement » envers notre chère patrie le Burkina Faso. « En regardant notre drapeau, souvenons-nous de ce qu’il représente : notre histoire, notre unité, notre dignité et notre espérance collective », a-t-il déclaré. Le représentant du PDS a dressé un bilan des principales activités menées au cours du mois d’août dans la commune. Il a notamment cité la célébration de la fête de l’Indépendance du Burkina Faso, le 5 août dernier qui, selon lui, a offert l’occasion de revisiter l’histoire nationale et de rendre hommage à ceux qui œuvrent à la construction et à la défense de la Nation. Moussa Sanou a également évoqué l’inauguration de l’extension de la centrale thermique de Bobo-Dioulasso et la campagne de destruction des gîtes larvaires dans le cadre de la lutte contre le paludisme. « Chaque espace assaini, chaque gîte larvaire détruit, chaque geste de prévention constitue une contribution à une ville plus saine », a-t-il soutenu, appelant les populations à faire de la protection du cadre de vie une responsabilité collective. Le président de la délégation spéciale de l’arrondissement n°3, Kisito Dabiré a souhaité la bienvenue aux participants et exprimé sa reconnaissance aux partenaires ayant accompagné l’arrondissement au cours des derniers mois. Il a lancé un appel aux bonnes volontés afin de soutenir les travaux de construction de la clôture de la mairie, dans l’optique de mieux sécuriser les lieux et préserver les aménagements réalisés. Agence d’Information du Burkina FG/OSAR/wis

items.title: Rentrée scolaire : des écoles publiques de Gemena reprennent avec des chantiers inachevés

items.title: Symboles et distinctions honorifiques dans l’AES: «N’ayons pas peur d’être différents»
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, le Camarade Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a reçu en audience, ce mercredi 2 septembre à Ouagadougou, une délégation des secrétaires généraux des Grandes Chancelleries des pays membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES). Présentée au Chef du Gouvernement par le Grand Chancelier des Ordres burkinabè, le Général de brigade à la retraite Pingrenoma Zagré, la délégation a recueilli les orientations du Premier ministre pour renforcer la transmission des valeurs nationales à la jeunesse et ancrer le système de reconnaissance du mérite dans les identités des peuples. Réunis dans la capitale burkinabè pour leur première rencontre technique, les secrétaires généraux des Grandes Chancelleries du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger échangent sur les cadres juridiques et institutionnels de leurs chancelleries afin de proposer les fondements d’un cadre commun de reconnaissance du mérite dans l’espace confédéral. Le Chef du Gouvernement a salué la tenue d’une telle rencontre, qui s’inscrit dans la dynamique de concertation prônée par les leaders des pays de l’AES. Pour le Camarade Premier ministre, les réflexions menées lors de cette rencontre doivent s’inscrire pleinement dans la démarche de rupture et d’affirmation de la souveraineté portée par les États de l’AES. Relevant que les pratiques de nombreuses chancelleries demeurent largement marquées par l’héritage colonial, il a appelé à des réformes qui accordent toute leur place aux références historiques, aux identités culturelles et aux valeurs propres aux peuples de la Confédération. « N’ayons pas peur d’être différents. Dans nos discours et dans les symboles, nous devons célébrer notre identité », a affirmé le Camarade Premier ministre. Il a ainsi invité ses interlocuteurs à puiser dans les traditions et les réalités socioculturelles des trois pays pour repenser les formes et les symboles de reconnaissance et de valorisation du mérite. Le Chef du Gouvernement a également exhorté les Grandes Chancelleries à mener une communication plus active, particulièrement en direction de la jeunesse. Il les a engagées à intégrer davantage la pédagogie et la sensibilisation dans leurs actions pour faire connaître les symboles et les valeurs de la Nation et en expliquer la signification, afin d’éveiller et de renforcer, chez les jeunes, l’amour de la Patrie et le respect de ses symboles. À la sortie de l’audience, le Grand Chancelier des Ordres burkinabè a précisé la finalité des réflexions en cours. « À terme, les conclusions issues de ces travaux devront permettre de définir les valeurs, les critères et les symboles devant encadrer l’attribution des distinctions honorifiques dans l’espace confédéral », a-t-il souligné. Pour sa part, Adama Traoré, chef de cabinet de la Grande Chancellerie du Mali, a rappelé que la reconnaissance du mérite occupait déjà une place importante dans les sociétés africaines, bien avant l’instauration des systèmes modernes de décorations. « Dans nos traditions, la reconnaissance du mérite existait au sein des communautés. Les hommes et les femmes qui faisaient preuve de courage, de bravoure ou qui se distinguaient par leur travail et leur contribution à la communauté étaient reconnus et valorisés », a-t-il expliqué. Selon lui, les travaux qui les réunissent à Ouagadougou aux côtés de leurs homologues burkinabè doivent permettre de remettre en lumière ces mécanismes traditionnels et de les adapter aux réalités contemporaines de la Confédération. L’ambition est également de promouvoir une reconnaissance du mérite qui valorise toute personne contribuant de manière remarquable, par son engagement, son travail ou sa bravoure, à l’édification de la Nation et de l’espace confédéral. Les orientations du Premier ministre invitent ainsi les Grandes Chancelleries à conjuguer reconnaissance du mérite et transmission des valeurs pour faire des distinctions honorifiques une expression de l’identité, du patriotisme et de la souveraineté des peuples de l’AES. DCRP/Primature L’article Symboles et distinctions honorifiques dans l’AES: «N’ayons pas peur d’être différents» est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Le calvaire des routes dégradées à Rufisque
items.description: Du rond-point Sipres, près de Zac Mbao, à la route Le Rivoli (Rue 1 de Rufisque Est), en passant par les Hlm, notamment à hauteur de la gare Pnr du Ter, automobilistes et usagers de la route souffrent le martyre à cause de la qualité défectueuse de ces infrastructures routières. RUFISQUE – La sortie 9 de l’autoroute à péage est très sollicitée aux heures de pointe, notamment à celle de la descente. Un flux important de véhicules emprunte cet axe stratégique vers Rufisque et, dans l’autre sens, Keur Massar, la banlieue dakaroise. À hauteur du rond-point Sipres, deux policiers, le sifflet à la bouche, régulent pour fluidifier le trafic. Parfois même, le rond-point est fermé, obligeant les véhicules à faire le grand détour pour accéder à la Zac Mbao. Loin des embouteillages, ce qui frappe de prime abord à l’attention, c’est le piteux état de la route. Nids de poule répertoriés à différents endroits. Cette situation rend le passage compliqué pour les véhicules et les contraint, bon gré mal gré, à lever le pied sur l’accélérateur. La plupart d’entre eux bifurquent près du terre-plein pour éviter les crevasses et autres imperfections dommageables. Le calvaire s’amplifie surtout en période d’hivernage, où ces trous béants sont couverts d’eau stagnante. Telle une zone de turbulence, à l’intérieur des voitures, notamment des lignes de bus Tata, les passagers s’accrochent et valsent entre les mouvements de roulis et de tangage incessants. Ces nids de poule jonchent également l’axe allant de la clinique Naby jusqu’à la cité Socabeg. Les véhicules font des slaloms pour les éviter. Pourtant, lors de la réception dudit tournant de 70 mètres entièrement refait en béton armé par la ville, le maire, Dr Oumar Cissé, avait pris l’engagement de combler les nids de poule qui longent cet axe. Jusqu’à présent, ces creux attendent des couches de revêtement. À l’instar de la cité Socabeg, l’axe Hlm jusqu’à la gare du Ter Pnr porte aussi les traces du caractère défectueux de la voie de circulation. « Une nuit, une voiture de transport en commun a failli renverser brutalement un conducteur de moto “Jakarta” en voulant éviter le dos d’âne sectionné », balance un usager. Ces ralentisseurs constituent également l’autre problème. La Route Le Rivoli, une cascade infernale À défaut d’être surdimensionnés ou sous-dimensionnés, certains dos d’âne situés aux Hlm sont coupés, laissant transparaître le fer. Avec les chantiers du boulevard Maurice Guèye, une voie de dégagement est indiquée par les tableaux à hauteur du rond-point Dioutiba pour les véhicules en partance pour Thiès. Au niveau du Pmu pour les paris, jusqu’aux abords du feu rouge, c’est le véritable parcours du combattant. La route, faite en béton armé, sous le poids des gros porteurs, s’est fortement dégradée (des affaissements de 5, voire 10 cm chaque 3 mètres, et une détérioration des raccordements des canaux secondaires relie au grand canal). Elle renvoie à une image de cascade et de rapides. Sur plus de 500 mètres, la mobilité demeure un véritable purgatoire. Les véhicules sont mis à rude épreuve. Avec dextérité, les conducteurs s’emploient difficilement à s’extirper de ce bourbier peu réconfortant. Chaque amortissement est accompagné de plaintes de passagers secoués. « L’état de cette route est très inquiétant. Le passage régulier des camions l’a fortement endommagé. Sous peu, je crains qu’aucun véhicule ne puisse passer par là », décrit Babacar Badiane, conducteur de moto « Jakarta ». Garé sur le côté, ce jeune conducteur souligne que cet axe est impraticable, surtout durant l’hivernage. « L’état pitoyable de la route a un impact négatif sur les organes de la voiture, les amortisseurs et autres… », regrette-t-il. D’ailleurs, certaines lignes Tata et autres véhicules passent par le marché pour contourner cette souffrance. C’est le cas du charretier, Ousmane. « Vu l’état actuel de la route, j’ai cessé de l’emprunter. C’est à la fois pénible pour le cheval, le conducteur et les clients. Ces secousses à répétition peuvent engendrer des douleurs corporelles », avance-t-il. Selon le cochet, cette voie secondaire était fluide et en bon état. Seulement, elle n’a pas su contenir l’important trafic journalier. À quelques encablures, des vendeurs étalent sur le canal fermé de l’ouest leurs marchandises : des chaussures pour hommes. De l’autre côté, entièrement pavé, les jeunes jouent au football, tandis que les personnes du troisième âge, assises sur les bancs aménagés, les observent. Serigne Khadim Gueye fait partie de la majorité qui réclame avec diligence l’ouverture du boulevard (sens Dakar-Thiès). « Nous sommes fatigués. Rufisque étouffe. Cette situation déteint sur l’économie de la ville », souligne-t-il. En attendant le bouclage définitif des travaux de Promovilles sur le boulevard Maurice Gueye et de son ouverture, les automobilistes et usagers de la route « Le Rivoli » devront encore prendre leur mal en patience. Sa rénovation ne se fera que par la suite. Mohamed DIÈNE (Correspondant)

items.title: SHC dismisses Mir Raza’s family’s plea for JIT to probe his murder
items.description: KARACHI: The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Wednesday dismissed a petition filed by the family of Mir Raza Ali seeking the formation of a joint investigation team (JIT) to probe his murder, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”. On Monday, the SHC reserved its verdict on a plea seeking the formation of a JIT in the case. A two-member bench, headed by Justice Adnanul Karim and comprising Justice Muhammad Jaffer Raza, had heard the petition. Ali’s family, which has raised questions about the case’s investigation and accused authorities of trying to bury the facts, had moved the SHC last week against a decision of the provincial government to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of a JIT instead. In a verdict issued today, the court ruled out directing the government to form a JIT and also declined to interfere with or supervise the ongoing criminal investigation. The verdict, authored by Justice Raza, framed three questions for determination. It asked whether the court’s constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 could be invoked to direct the formation of a JIT. Whether the court could substitute, supervise or affect the statutory criminal investigation and the report under Section 173 of the CrPC through Article 199; and whether interference was warranted in the absence of a Gazette notification under the Sindh Tribunals of Inquiry Ordinance, 1969. In his judgment, Justice Raza maintained that, at the time of the judgment, the first information report (FIR) did not contain any offence under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA), 1997. “Even if the FIR had included offences under the ATA, 1997, constitution of a JIT under that provision would remain the prerogative of the government,” Justice Raza said. The petitioners had also argued that Article 199 empowered the high court to monitor an investigation to ensure that it was fair, impartial and effective. The court disagreed, relying on a earlier Supreme Court judgment. Justice Raza also quoted the SC’s ruling in Sughran Bibi vs the State as saying: “Such an approach sets up the courts as monitors or supervisors of the investigation, a role which the law forbids and the precedent loathes.” “It is well settled that this court ought not to interfere with the ongoing investigation, and/or assume the role of an investigator,” the judgment said. The court, however, maintained that the petitioners were at “liberty to avail all remedies available to them under the law to ensure that the investigation is carried out in a manner which is fair, impartial, efficient and transparent”. Furthermore, the court deliberately refrained from recording the competing factual allegations made by the parties, noting that doing so could affect the ongoing investigation, the verdict said. Justice Raza observed that the petitioner had not seriously contested the formation of a single-member commission to probe Mir Raza’s murder and had expressed confidence in it as ancillary relief. “Even otherwise, we are not inclined to hinder or make any observation concerning proceedings pending before the Commission,” he asserted. The case The case has been mired in controversy since the beginning. While Ali’s family was convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police had initially built the case around the possibility that he died by suicide. Days after the recovery of Ali’s body, Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Sumaiyya Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and later approached the SHC. The petition was filed on August 24 in objection to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case” in place of the commission. The commission held the first hearing on Friday, and has summoned medico-legal officer Osama Sheikh, who had performed Ali’s first autopsy. It also issued notices to the deceased’s family, their lawyer and a provincial government focal person.
